title: Discrimination
summary: Why discrimination is hard to spot in one's own life, what it does to the mind and body of its targets, and four practical ways to reduce it.

lesson.title: The bias you cannot see
lesson.hook: Ask a group of women if women in their company are treated unfairly and many say yes. Ask each one if she personally is, and most say no. Both answers cannot be fully true.

slides.heading: Common, yet hard to spot
slides.body:
Discrimination is widespread, yet one of the biggest obstacles to removing it is surprising: people struggle to **detect it in their own lives**.

If a job interview goes badly, was it your answers, the interviewer's mood, or your surname? A single event has many possible causes. That uncertainty lets discrimination hide in plain sight.

steps.title: No control group
steps.detail: You cannot rerun your life as a member of a privileged group to compare the treatment you would have got (Fiske, 1998).

steps.title: Single cases are explained away
steps.detail: One incident has many excuses; patterns only show when many cases are pooled (Crosby, 1984).

steps.title: Denial protects us
steps.detail: Admitting mistreatment means feeling wronged and out of control, so people may play it down (Ruggiero & Taylor, 1997).

slides.question: Crosby (1984) argued discrimination is easier to detect with:
slides.why: One case can always be explained away; aggregated evidence reveals the pattern.

slides.heading: Group yes, me no
slides.body:
Because of these barriers, women and minority members are **quicker to see their **group** being treated unfairly than to say **they personally** are (Crosby, 1984; Taylor, Wright & Porter, 1994).

This gap is called the **personal/group discrimination discrepancy**. It does not mean they are wrong about the group; it means each person finds it easier to excuse their own case.

slides.heading: The bank's promotion list
slides.story: At a Lagos bank, Halima notices women rarely make branch manager. She tells friends women are held back there. But when she herself is passed over, she tells herself the other candidate had better targets. Only when the union counts promotions over five years does the pattern become undeniable.
slides.takeaway: Halima sees group discrimination but excuses her own case; pooled data reveal what single cases hide.

slides.heading: The cost to targets' health
slides.body:
Studying discrimination from the **target's side** shows real harm. Clark and colleagues (1999) described racism as a chronic **stressor**.

Williams and colleagues (1997) linked the discrimination Black Americans report to poorer **self-rated health**, lower **psychological wellbeing** and more **days off sick**. Like any long-running stress, it wears down mind and body.

slides.heading: Stereotype threat and blood pressure
slides.body:
**Stereotype threat** is the worry of confirming a negative stereotype about your group. Steele and Aronson (1995) showed it can lower test performance.

It also reaches the body. Blascovich and colleagues (2001) found Black participants' **blood pressure rose** under stereotype threat, and McNeilly and colleagues (1995) found similar rises when people faced **racist provocation**.

slides.question: Taylor, Wright and Porter (1994) found minority members tend to report:
slides.why: This is the personal/group discrimination discrepancy: people see their group targeted more readily than themselves.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: A common question: 'why is discrimination difficult to detect at the individual level?' Give all three reasons with their authors. Objectives twist it with scenarios of someone denying their own mistreatment. Also expect health consequences with names: Williams et al. (1997), Blascovich et al. (2001).
slides.sampleQuestion: Which of the following is NOT a reason individuals find it hard to detect discrimination? (a) they cannot act as their own control group (b) single cases are easily explained away (c) denial protects a sense of control (d) discrimination never affects health
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (d): it is false and not a detection barrier. Name Fiske (1998), Crosby (1984) and Ruggiero & Taylor (1997) for the three real reasons.

points: Discrimination is common but hard to detect in one's own life.
No control group, single cases excused, and protective denial hide it.
People see group discrimination more than personal discrimination.
Discrimination acts as a stressor that harms health.
Stereotype threat and racist incidents can raise blood pressure.

questions.stem: One of the greatest barriers to removing discrimination is that:
options: It is hard to detect at the individual level
questions.explanation: Despite being common, discrimination is hard for individuals to spot in their own lives.

questions.stem: The tendency to see more discrimination against one's group than against oneself is the:
questions.explanation: That gap is the personal/group discrimination discrepancy, linked with Crosby and with Taylor, Wright and Porter.

questions.stem: Stereotype threat refers to:
options: Worry about confirming a negative stereotype of one's group
questions.explanation: Stereotype threat is the fear of confirming a negative group stereotype, which can affect performance and the body.

questions.stem: Fiske (1998) noted that individuals cannot easily detect discrimination because they:
options: Cannot serve as their own control group
questions.explanation: You cannot relive events as a member of a privileged group to compare treatment. Denial is a separate reason from Ruggiero and Taylor.

questions.stem: Ruggiero and Taylor (1997) suggested some people deny personal discrimination in order to:
options: Avoid feeling mistreated and lacking control
questions.explanation: Denial guards self-esteem and a sense of control over one's life.

questions.stem: Williams and colleagues (1997) linked reported discrimination among Black Americans to:
questions.explanation: They found poorer self-rated health, lower wellbeing and more sick days.

questions.stem: Ngozi believes female engineers in her firm are underpaid, yet insists her own lower salary is due to her negotiating skills. This illustrates:
questions.explanation: She sees discrimination against her group but not against herself, the classic discrepancy.

questions.stem: A union proves discrimination by comparing five years of promotion records across ethnic groups. This approach works because:
options: Aggregated evidence reveals patterns single cases hide
questions.explanation: Crosby (1984) noted discrimination is easier to detect with pooled evidence, as individual cases can be explained away.

questions.stem: Before a maths test, students are reminded that 'girls are weak at maths'. The girls' blood pressure rises and scores drop. This reflects:
questions.explanation: Fear of confirming a negative group stereotype is stereotype threat, which can affect both performance and physiology.

questions.stem: All of the following are reasons discrimination is hard to detect individually EXCEPT:
options: Denial protects a sense of control
Single cases can be explained away
questions.explanation: Discrimination rarely leaves clear written proof; that is part of why it is hard to see. The other three are the recognised barriers.

questions.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Blascovich et al. (2001): stereotype threat and blood pressure
Williams et al. (1997): no control group
questions.explanation: Blascovich and colleagues linked stereotype threat with raised blood pressure. Crosby studied denial of personal discrimination and pooled evidence.

questions.stem: Clark and colleagues (1999) describe racism mainly as a:
questions.explanation: They modelled racism as a stressor with biological and psychological effects.

questions.stem: I. People cannot test how they would be treated as a privileged-group member. II. Pooled data reveal discrimination better than single cases. III. Minority members usually report more personal than group discrimination. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and II are correct. III reverses the finding: people report more group than personal discrimination.

questions.stem: A researcher finds minority employees rate discrimination against their group as high but their own as low. The most likely explanation is:
options: Single personal cases are easier to explain away and denial protects control
questions.explanation: The discrepancy arises because personal incidents can be excused and denial preserves a sense of control. It does not show discrimination is absent.

questions.stem: Why do findings on blood pressure under stereotype threat matter for the study of discrimination?
options: They show bias can harm physical health, not only feelings
They show discrimination only affects mood
They show targets cause their own stress
questions.explanation: Physiological effects show discrimination has bodily costs, supporting the stressor view. They say nothing about stereotypes being accurate.

lesson.title: Four ways to push back
lesson.hook: If humans are so quick to stereotype, is discrimination just human nature? Research says the tendency is real, but so is our power to override it.

slides.heading: Empathy: step into their shoes
slides.body:
**Empathy** has a big practical advantage: it is fairly **easy to apply**. Becoming empathic towards targets of discrimination means asking simple questions:

- If this happened to me, what would I feel?
- What might this person be feeling now?
- What could explain their behaviour?

Taking another person's perspective makes it harder to treat them as just a member of a category.

slides.heading: Role-play: rehearse the response
slides.body:
Many people want to object when someone makes a prejudiced remark but freeze in the moment. **Plous (2000)** used **role-playing** exercises so students could practise responding effectively to prejudiced comments.

Rehearsing a calm reply, like 'I don't think that's fair to say about a whole group', makes it far more likely you will actually say it when it counts.

slides.question: Plous (2000) used role-playing mainly to help people:
slides.why: His role-play exercise trained people to answer prejudiced remarks well in real situations.

slides.heading: Laws, rules and norms
slides.body:
**Oskamp (2000)** pointed to a structural route: **laws, regulations and social norms that require fair treatment**.

Laws change behaviour even before attitudes catch up. Over time, as fair treatment becomes normal, attitudes often follow. In Nigeria, the **federal character principle** in the Constitution aims to spread public appointments fairly across states, a legal tool against one group dominating.

slides.heading: Expose the inconsistency
slides.body:
Most people see themselves as fair. When shown that their **values, attitudes and behaviour do not match** the ideal of equality they claim, they feel uncomfortable and change.

Milton **Rokeach** (1971) used this 'value confrontation': people shown the gap between valuing freedom and caring little about others' equality were still **backing civil rights more strongly over a year afterwards**. Few methods last that long.

steps.title: Empathy
steps.detail: Imagine the target's feelings and situation.

steps.title: Laws and norms
steps.detail: Require fair treatment through rules and social expectations (Oskamp, 2000).

steps.title: Inconsistency awareness
steps.detail: Show people the gap between their values and behaviour for lasting change.

slides.heading: The class rep's challenge
slides.story: In a WhatsApp group, a classmate jokes that students from one region 'only pass by sorting'. Tolu, who practised responses in a workshop, replies calmly: 'We all claim we believe in merit. Is it fair to judge a whole region by a rumour?' The joke stops, and later two people message Tolu to agree.
slides.takeaway: Tolu combined a rehearsed response with pointing out the gap between stated values and the remark.

slides.heading: Bias can be overcome
slides.body:
Humans may be '**homo stereotypus**', creatures quick to categorise and stereotype. But the same research shows we can **override** these tendencies when **motivated** (Blair, 2002; Fiske, 2000; Monteith & Voils, 2001).

It takes **awareness and deliberate effort**. Even automatic stereotypes turn out to be malleable. Bias is a habit, and habits can be changed.

slides.question: Which method produced support for civil rights that lasted more than a year?
options: Showing people inconsistencies between their values and behaviour
slides.why: Value confrontation, making people aware their behaviour clashed with their equality ideals, had long-lasting effects.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: 'Mention and explain four ways of reducing discrimination' is a classic short essay. Name the four, attach an author, and give a Nigerian example. In objectives, watch for EXCEPT questions where the odd option sounds positive, like 'greater support for civil rights', which is an outcome, not a method.
slides.sampleQuestion: All are ways of reducing discrimination EXCEPT: (a) laws mandating fair treatment (b) empathy towards targets (c) awareness of value-behaviour inconsistency (d) greater support for civil rights
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (d): support for civil rights is a result of reducing prejudice, not a technique. The other three are methods.

points: Empathy: easy to apply; imagine how the target feels.
Role-play helps people answer prejudiced comments (Plous, 2000).
Laws, regulations and norms mandate fair treatment (Oskamp, 2000).
Exposing value-behaviour inconsistency brings lasting change.
Bias can be overcome with awareness, effort and motivation.

questions.stem: Which method of reducing discrimination involves asking 'If I were in their place, what would I feel?'
questions.explanation: Imagining the target's feelings is empathy. Role-playing rehearses responses to prejudiced remarks.

questions.stem: Oskamp (2000) highlighted reducing discrimination through:
options: Laws, regulations and norms mandating fair treatment
questions.explanation: Oskamp pointed to rules and norms requiring fair treatment.

questions.stem: The method credited with practising responses to prejudiced comments is:
questions.explanation: Plous (2000) used role-play to help people respond effectively.

questions.stem: A major practical advantage of empathy as a way to reduce discrimination is that it:
questions.explanation: Empathy can be practised by anyone, any time, by taking the target's perspective.

questions.stem: The longest-lasting reduction in discrimination described came from:
options: Awareness of inconsistencies between values and behaviour
questions.explanation: People confronted with the gap between their values and behaviour showed more support for civil rights over a year later.

questions.stem: The idea that humans are 'homo stereotypus' means they are:
options: Predisposed to stereotyping but able to overcome it
questions.explanation: We are prone to stereotyping, but research shows motivation and effort can override it.

questions.stem: A company trains staff by acting out scenes where a customer makes an ethnic slur and staff practise replying. This uses:
questions.explanation: Acting out and rehearsing responses is role-playing, the method used by Plous.

questions.stem: Nigeria's federal character principle, requiring fair spread of public appointments across states, reflects which approach?
options: Laws and regulations mandating fair treatment
questions.explanation: It is a legal rule designed to ensure fair representation, matching Oskamp's structural route.

questions.stem: A lecturer shows students that they rate equality highly yet support policies that exclude some groups. The students later show more support for equal rights. This illustrates:
options: Awareness of inconsistency between values and behaviour
questions.explanation: Exposing the gap between values and actions creates discomfort that motivates change.

questions.stem: All of the following are ways of reducing discrimination EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Support for civil rights is an outcome of reduced prejudice, not a method. The others are techniques.

questions.stem: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Rokeach: value confrontation with lasting effects
questions.explanation: Rokeach's value confrontation produced long-lasting attitude change. Plous used role-play and Oskamp discussed laws and norms.

questions.stem: Why can laws reduce discrimination even when attitudes have not yet changed?
options: Laws regulate behaviour, and attitudes often follow as norms shift
questions.explanation: Laws act on behaviour first; as fair treatment becomes normal, attitudes tend to follow.

questions.stem: I. Empathy is relatively easy to apply. II. Automatic stereotypes cannot be changed. III. Motivation and effort can reduce bias. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and III are supported. II is wrong: Blair and others show automatic stereotypes are malleable.

questions.stem: A researcher wants a reduction in discrimination that is still visible a year later. The research suggests the best choice is:
options: Making people aware that their behaviour contradicts their own equality values
questions.explanation: Value-behaviour inconsistency produced effects lasting over a year. Separation and stereotype reminders would not reduce discrimination.

questions.stem: Which statement best summarises research on overcoming prejudice?
options: Bias is fixed by nature and cannot change
With awareness, deliberate effort and motivation, bias can be reduced
Bias disappears once people are educated
questions.explanation: Blair, Fiske and Monteith show bias is malleable when people are motivated and aware. Education alone or laws alone are not the whole story.
